title: Software is slow because of bad design, not slow languages
content:
Many people are saying that AI will make software faster by rewriting it in faster languages, but this isn’t generally true. Most programs cannot be meaningfully sped up by rewriting them in C or Rust.

How can this be true? Some languages are orders-of-magnitude faster than others: for instance, C can be fifty times faster than Python. Won’t rewriting my Python program in C thus make it fifty times faster? No, it won’t. Software performance is usually dominated by I/O, not the speed of the language. Where language speed matters, most slow languages already have popular libraries that allow them to unlock C-like speed. In general, performance is a matter of design, not of language choice.

Most real programs are I/O-bound

Consider a simple CRUD website with a database. For any given request, 50% of the request time1 might be spent querying the database: to fetch the current user, the record being asked for, any relevant user memberships or settings, and so on. Rewriting that website in C can only speed up that other 50%, which puts a hard ceiling on the improvements you can make2. At best, you’ll make requests twice as fast (probably closer to 1.5x in practice). That’s not bad, but it’s nowhere near an order-of-magnitude speedup.

In other words, most real programs are “I/O-bound”: they spend most of their time waiting for data to be input or output somewhere, as opposed to “CPU-bound” programs that spend most of their time actively doing things. I/O-bound programs don’t just have to rely on a database. Often programs have to wait on some third-party API, or on writing or reading data to disk. You could speed the code in curl up by 100x and you probably wouldn’t even notice, because curl spends all of its time waiting on the network.

Slow languages already delegate work to fast languages

What about work that is obviously not I/O-bound? For instance, wikis have to turn stored markdown into renderable HTML3. Wouldn’t rewriting that in a faster language cause a massive speedup? It would! That’s why applications that do that use libraries like cmark-gfm that call out to fast languages for markdown rendering. In general, most slow languages can write very fast programs by invoking this kind of library. Python is famously a slow language, but it’s a competitive choice for CPU-bound workloads like machine learning and mathematics, because it has a healthy set of libraries that let it offload these workloads to fast C code. If a Python program spends 80% of its time doing matrix multiplications on a GPU, you are very unlikely to be able to speed it up by rewriting it in C, because those matrix multiplications are already happening in tightly-optimized C or assembly code.

Of course, some programs do in fact do a lot of CPU-bound work in slow languages. If a program has not had much engineering attention, there will probably be a lot of low-hanging fruit. But these programs are often unimportant: if they were important, someone would have gone in and optimized them already, before AI made it (relatively) easy. That doesn’t mean it’s impossible to find a useful program to rewrite. Actual Computer recently rewrote tiktoken in assembly, providing a significant4 speedup. However, you’re not going to revolutionize some field of computing like this. Even fast tokenization is only useful on the margins, because time spent in tokenization is a fraction of the time spent in inference.

Speeding up software typically involves a redesign

Despite all this, I think most software is far slower than it could be. I’m optimistic about the potential (with or without AI) to significantly speed up commonly-used software. But I think most of these speedups will come from redesigning the program, not rewriting it in a faster language.

In a 2018 post, Bryan Cantrill described trying to rewrite a C program into Rust. It was difficult because the carefully-optimized design of the C program did not play well with the Rust borrow checker. Giving up, he simply wrote the program in Rust in the naive way, expecting a 20% slowdown or worse. Instead, it was 30% faster. The reasons boil down to Rust’s internal preference for a B-tree over a binary search tree, which happens to be a more cache-efficient data structure. So even in a largely CPU-bound workload, in the hands of someone very skilled at writing fast C, performance is dominated by design, not by language speed.

This matches my own experience in higher-level languages. When I think of the significant speedups I’ve managed, they’re almost exclusively redesigns of the software to do less work:

  • Caching a slow operation (typically an external API call)
  • Performing slow operations asynchronously, either in a background job or out of the request/response lifecycle
  • Performing operations in parallel instead of sequentially (sometimes breaking up large operations in order to do this)
  • Replacing a set of SQL queries with a single SQL query (fixing N+1 problems)
  • Replacing a slow SQL query with a fast SQL query
  • Skipping unnecessary slow operations (e.g. in a paginated view, only fetch ancillary data from entities that are on the current page)

All of these strategies are completely unrelated to how fast the language is. In fact, writing in a slow higher-level language can make it much easier to optimize the code, because you can see at a glance what the program is doing. If (for some reason) I had first rewritten the web server in assembly, I would have a much harder time noticing the N+1 query, or the fact that we could move an API call into a job, and so on.

Conclusion

Right now everyone is asking their AI agents to rewrite programs in Rust or C or assembly. This is fun, but it’s not a serious attempt at optimization. The set of programs that can be meaningfully sped up by this kind of rewrite is very narrow.

If you want to make everything faster with AI — and you should! — you ought instead to be asking your agent to profile programs, identify hotspots, and suggest ways to redesign what the program does. Occasionally you may run into a hotspot that is truly CPU-bound and cannot be refactored to do less work. In these rare cases, rewriting that section in a faster language will help. But simply rewriting from the start will be far less successful than most people imagine.

There are many good reasons to rewrite software in a different language: portability, efficiency, maintainability, and so on. But in terms of raw speed, you’re better off focusing on the program’s design.

  1. This might seem ridiculously high (if you typically work with slow languages or CPU-bound workloads), or ridiculously low (if you don’t). In my experience it’s at least in the ballpark for interpreted languages.

  2. This is formally called Amdahl’s law.

    ↩

  3. Why not just store the HTML? You can, but sometimes the content of the HTML differs per-user (and even if you store the HTML you have to convert it at least once).

    ↩

  4. They claim 4-23x faster than tiktoken and it was indeed ~5x faster on my laptop — though arguably this speedup comes from a redesign to avoid the dependency on regex, not on any intrinsic slowness of Rust with Python bindings.

title: Apple Highlights 50+ iPhone Apps That Have Already Been Optimized for the Duo
content:
Apple Newsroom:

New editorial collections for iPhone Duo apps and games will go live on the App Store this Friday, with additional app updates rolling out throughout the year. Apps optimized for iPhone Duo are easy to identify with a Made for iPhone Duo badge on product pages across the storefront.

This story highlights dozens of apps that have been optimized. This sort of transition happens every time Apple introduces a major screen change. It happened with the iPhone X in 2017, it happened when the iPhone 6 added a Plus size, it happened when the iPhone 5 changed the aspect ratio from 3:2 to 16:9, and, most memorably of all, it happened when the iPhone 4 went retina. Every time this happens it sucks to some varying degree of suckiness to use apps that haven’t been optimized. And soon enough, all apps still under active development get updated.

Developers know that iPhone users care how apps look and work. iPhone users will switch to competing apps for something like this. I stopped checking Mastodon on my phone for the last week and half because Ivory isn’t optimized. I stopped reading my messages on Signal — I just wait until I’m back at my desk. If I bought a Duo, I’d literally stop using Signal if they don’t update their app soon. Life’s too short to use shitty apps. iPhone developers get that.

Out of all those transitions I listed above, my gut feeling is that there are more third-party apps ready to go on day one for the Duo than for any of those previous transitions. No, it’s not all apps. Some of the apps that aren’t yet updated are quite popular, and others are ones that users can’t easily just switch away from (like, say, your bank’s app). But developer support is not a problem for the Duo. If anything the launch of the Duo has exemplified better than any event in iPhone history just how different the iPhone and Android developer communities are. “Flagship” Android foldables have been out for over 7 years and developer support for them today remains nothing close to developer support for the Duo — and the Duo doesn’t even launch until tomorrow.

 ★

title: Productivity
content:
I'd say in a given week I probably only do about fifteen minutes of real, actual, work. — Office Space

I was watching a video where a guy said he has 8 agents working in the background. He was stressed out and was trying to "get shit done." At one point he said "I have no time to myself."

That was very confusing. Let's assume for a second that the AI agents were doing all the work for him. Maybe it was some tedious work that would have taken him so much time to do manually. Now, he doesn't have to do the work because someone else is doing it. Why is he still busy?

The Future we were promised

It seems like the goal of productivity is to reduce the amount of work needed to create a set of results. But the moment you create the same results in less time, you are incentivised to use the new gained time to produce even more results.

You will rest when you grow up — My Mom.

But now that we are grown up, our employer changed the tune just a bit:

You will rest when you are dead.

title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
content:
In the hours following the release of CVE-2026-93479 for the project NGINX, site reliability workers and systems administrators scrambled to desperately rebuild and patch all their systems to fix a heap buffer overflow in worker script evaluation triggered by crafted requests when regex map captures are referenced before the map output, or when a non-cacheable variable is used in certain string expressions, causing worker restarts and potentially code execution if ASLR is disabled or bypassed. This is due to the affected components being written in C, the only programming language where these vulnerabilities regularly happen. "This was a terrible tragedy, but sometimes these things just happen and there's nothing anyone can do to stop them," said programmer Mr. Mariano Franecki, echoing statements expressed by hundreds of thousands of programmers who use the only language where 90% of the world's memory safety vulnerabilities have occurred in the last 50 years, and whose projects are 20 times more likely to have security vulnerabilities. "It's a shame, but what can we do? There really isn't anything we can do to prevent memory safety vulnerabilities from happening if the programmer doesn't want to write their code in a robust manner." At press time, users of the only programming language in the world where these vulnerabilities regularly happen once or twice per quarter for the last eight years were referring to themselves and their situation as "helpless."

title: Working around a strange Python problem
content:
A Python script that worked a few days ago wouldn’t work today. I suspect it might have something to do with my updating everything I could think of in response to recent security breaches.

I got an error message that said

error: The script contains multiple PEP 723 metadata blocks

I searched on what that means, then took out the blank line in my header

#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script

# /// script
# dependencies = ["pyperclip"]
# ///

but I still got the same error message.

The script in question copies miscellaneous snippets of text to the clipboard for me. One of those snippets is the header block that uv requires. The script contains the header block marker # ///, and that was the source of the problem.

According to Grok

The PEP 723 parser is purely textual (it uses a regex that scans the whole file). It does not understand Python syntax, so the # /// sequences inside your triple-quoted string are treated as a second metadata block.

It suggested changing my quoted string to use # / / / and then take out the extra spaces:

"""#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
# / / / script
# dependencies = ["numpy", "matplotlib"]
# / / /
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
""".replace("# / / /", "# ///")

This is a dirty hack, but it works.

The post Working around a strange Python problem first appeared on John D. Cook.

title: Script dependencies with Nix
content:
In the theme of NixOS enabling fearlessness, here’s a way I use Nix on other Linux distributions to sleep better at night: managing dependencies of simple scripts.

This way of using Nix is for everyone, not just those willing to try NixOS. We’ll look at it first for a Python script, and then see how it can be adapted to any other language.

I wanted to create a script that would read the verbatim content of my articles out loud to me with a synthesised voice. One of the more convenient ways to do this is with Python, where I’ve heard good things about Trafilatura for extracting the contents out of a web page, filtering on types of content, etc.

But Trafilatura is a third-party Python dependency. Those suck because they break your scripts when you so much as glance sideways at pip. The code also ended up depending on aplay, which is a system dependency, making it two different sources of future breakage. A couple of years ago, I would probably have judged that to be too much maintenance, so I wouldn’t have created the script. Fortunately, now I know about Nix.

title: NYC, New Webinar, Differential Testing
content:
Been a while! Man, it's so much harder to write essays for a newsletter when I have a full time job writing essays for a company.

So three bits of housekeeping first of all:

  • As of last month I now live in NYC! Let me know if you want to get coffee or have me swing by an office or something.
  • I'm back on Twitter. Do not mourn me for I do not deserve it.

  • My first big Antithesis deliverable is coming out next Thursday, and it's a webinar on property-based testing. What's going to make this one interesting is that it's about property testing web applications. I've got this crazy idea that the main way to make randomized testing accessible and useful is to focus on state-based system invariants as opposed to algebraic laws and roundtrip properties. Send it to webdevs you know!1

Anyway, to make this actually a newsletter and not just a bunch of updates, one thing I've been thinking about recently is nondeterministic differential testing. Say we have a python program and we tell a slopinator to convert it to rust. How do we know that it didn't change the program's behavior?

For a totally deterministic program, this is straightforward differential testing: feed inputs into both and compare the results. Let's scrap out a quick notation and say that A -> (x, y) represents an execution where we input A, and observe that the original program output x and the new program output y. So A -> (1, 1) means that the programs agree on input A, while B -> (1, 2) means they get different values for input B. The programs are different if we observe a single disagreement, meaning we can increase our relative confidence in our translating by trying an increasing number of inputs.

That's the base case, anyway. But this only really works because there's no point in repeating observations on the same input. If the program is nondeterministic, we can get situations like this:

A -> (200 OK, 408 request timeout)
A -> (200, 200)

Are the program different? We can't be sure! If the original system always returns 200, then they're different. But we don't know that for sure from the observations we have! Maybe a third observation will give us A -> (408, 200). In other words, a table of what we know, given an observation and level of uncertainty:

Deterministic? A -> (x, y) A -> (x, x)
Yes definitely different ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
No ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Once you need mutiple observations you're already dealing with the mess known as hyperproperties. But we can make it even more complicated than that! What if we have this set of observations:

A -> (200, 408)
A -> (200, 200)
A -> (408, 408)

You could argue the two programs agree on observations of A. Not so fast! One thing we haven't seen is A -> (408, 200). Maybe there's no world where the old program times out but the new program gets 200. Even though they get the same set of nondeterministic outputs, one can still be more reliable than the other. This makes it much harder to show the two programs are the same: if you observe A -> (x, y), it's not enough to observe A -> (z, x), you have to specifically observe A -> (y, x).

Okay, but what if the relative rate of values in observations matter? What if the new program gets a 408 timeout 100x as often? What if your LLM converted a fair coin flip to an unfair coin flip? Then even if we see A -> (H, T) and A -> (T, H), we still have a program divergence.

In short, two challenges with nondeterministic differential testing are 1) we can't conclude a difference from a single divergent observation and 2) the concept of "difference" is way murkier than in deterministic programs. Though TBF even with deterministic programs the same output can be a divergence if one takes a lot longer. It all depends on how you define correctness!

(I think in most cases, we can get away with just showing two nondeterministic programs produce the same set of values. That's still pretty hard, but at least it's not messing with probability.)
